knowledge_point.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Product  at a Given Point

question.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(2 x^{3})\cdot (\sin{\left(x \right)})$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=2 x^{3}$ and $v(x)=\sin{\left(x \right)}.$ Then, we have

$$
u'(x)=6 x^{2},\quad v'(x)=\cos{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} &=uv'(x)+vu'(x) \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(2 x^{3})\cdot (\cos{\left(x \right)}) \\ &{}+(\sin{\left(x \right)})\cdot (6 x^{2})\end{aligned} \\ &=2 x^{2} \left(x \cos{\left(x \right)} + 3 \sin{\left(x \right)}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_{x=\frac{\pi}{2}} &=\begin{aligned}&(2 \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{3})\cdot (\cos{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)}) \\ &{}+(\sin{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)})\cdot (6 \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{2})\end{aligned} \\ &=\left(\frac{\pi^{3}}{4}\right)\cdot (0)+(1)\cdot \left(\frac{3 \pi^{2}}{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{3 \pi^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $\frac{3 \pi^{2}}{2}.$
